annotations.text:
WORTH TELLING -- what this is

You send from the desk. One picture per customer per fortnight. Site stage goes on the record. Everything on this canvas follows from those three.

THE ALGORITHM IS FIVE RULES, AND THE RAIL SHOWS THEM. There is no model. At forty-five customers a trained model has nothing to learn from and cannot say why it picked anything; five rules read off your own invoices, stock book and follow-ups are more accurate AND every row can explain itself -- which matters, because you are the one pressing send.

A CUSTOMER IS ON THE LIST ONLY IF ONE OF SIX THINGS IS TRUE ABOUT THEM:
1. DUE BY RHYTHM -- they buy a line every N days, at least three times, and the next is within 3 days.
2. THEY ASKED -- a follow-up or sourcing ask, and it has come in. Highest priority: it is a recommendation they requested.
3. PRICE DOWN FOR THEM -- what they buy now costs at least 5% less than THEY last paid. The strongest sentence in the trade.
4. SITE STAGE -- their build moved to a stage they have not bought for yet. Sized from their last order.
5. COME BACK -- one order, then silence past 21 days.
6. COMPANION -- only ever as the third frame, never the reason: what other orders of this size carried, from your own invoices, with the count shown.

ONE REASON PER CUSTOMER, THE DEAREST. The runners-up are listed in the open row and wait a fortnight -- and if the customer buys the thing anyway, the reason stops being true and goes.

RANKED by typical order x how sure the reason is. "They asked" is certain. A 3-order rhythm is less sure than a 7-order one. The screen says the formula in its header.

HELD BACK, AND NAMED. Told inside 14 days, chased inside 7, past terms, no phone number. Somebody you are chasing for money does not also get a picture of cement.

NOTHING SENDS ITSELF. Share opens WhatsApp with the GIF attached and the customer's chat chosen; you press send. The app writes it down as told when you do, and the fortnight starts from then.

DID IT WORK is the honest measure: bought within 14 days of being told, per reason. It is not proof -- Kato would have bought cement anyway -- but it is what the books can say, and reasons that never convert sink on their own.

THE PICTURE -- 600x800, four frames, ~6.5 seconds, loops

Built on-device from a canvas, encoded to GIF in the browser (gif.js), under 1 MB. No server. The product photo comes from Media; where there is none the frame shows the name large and no placeholder box.

FRAME 1 -- THE HOOK, IN THEIR NAME. One sentence a shopkeeper would say: "Kato -- your cement is due about Thursday." Navy, because it is the shop's colour and the one a WhatsApp thumbnail shows.

FRAME 2 -- WHAT, HOW MANY, AT WHAT PRICE, AND WHY. Their quantity, not a default. Their price, with "your price" said out loud. And the reason line in verdigris, because it is the thing that makes this feel like a person who knows them rather than a bot: "Because you take 40 every 18 days, and the site is at walling."

FRAME 3 -- THE COMPANION, WITH ITS EVIDENCE. "11 of 14 orders this size carried nails too. Not a guess." The count is on the frame deliberately: it is what separates this from every other shop's promo.

FRAME 4 -- ONE ACTION, ONE NUMBER. Reply YES. Same price, delivered Thursday. Your own number, named as yours. Oxide, once, on the frame that asks.

WHAT IS NEVER ON A FRAME: a discount you have not decided to give, a delivery day the trips screen does not hold, stock you do not have, a product with no photo pretending to have one. Every figure comes off the same books as the register.

THE TEXT IN THE MESSAGE is one line the app drafts and you can change: "Kato -- cement due Thursday, 40 bags at your price. Reply YES and it is set aside." The GIF is the message; the text is for the notification preview.

SITE STAGE -- the input you agreed to add

One dropdown and a date on the customer form. Seven values: Not a site (a retailer), Foundation, Walling, Roofing, Plumbing & electrical, Finishing, Done.

WHY IT PREDICTS BEST: a build goes in an order, and each stage buys a different shelf. A rhythm can only say "more of the same"; a stage says what comes NEXT, before they have bought any of it. That is the one thing no figure in the books can do.

WHAT EACH STAGE BUYS is read from your own invoices where the stage was known at the time, and from the list on the form until there are enough of them -- and the screen says which it used.

IT GOES STALE BY ITSELF. The date is what makes it safe: a stage older than 60 days stops counting until it is confirmed, so a site that finished in July does not get roofing sheets in September. The rail lists who to ask.

OPEN: whether an agent in the field can set it, or only the desk. I have drawn desk-only, as you said for sending; setting a stage is lower stakes and the field is where the answer is.

NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. THE 14-DAY MEASURE. Bought within 14 days counts as a win. Too short and a fortnightly buyer never counts; too long and everything counts. Editable in the rail beside the other rules.

2. WHAT "YES" DOES. I have drawn "Reply YES and it is set aside" -- which means when they reply, YOU create the order. If you would rather the picture said "call us" or nothing, it is one frame.

3. THE COMPANION'S THRESHOLD. "11 of 14" is worth showing; "3 of 14" is not. I have drawn it only where the majority of same-size orders carried the line.

4. WHETHER TO SHOW A PRICE AT ALL. For a customer whose last price is older than 90 days, "your price" may be a price you no longer give. The rule I drew: show the CURRENT price, and say "your price" only if it is unchanged since they last paid.

5. THE PHONE. You send from the desk, so the phone is drawn as look-then-share: a card per customer, the film strip, one accent in the dock. If the phone should be strictly read-only, the dock goes.
